interactions: Amphotericin B + flucytosine: amphotericin nephrotoxicity reduces flucytosine clearance and raises flucytosine levels; monitor creatinine and adjust flucytosine to renal function (flucytosine levels where available).
Fluconazole: inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19; review every drug added later, including antiretrovirals and antituberculous drugs (rifampicin lowers fluconazole exposure).
Nystatin oral suspension: no clinically significant interaction expected.

output.summary: No contraindication to the proposed induction agents. Amphotericin B reduces flucytosine clearance, so renal function guides the flucytosine dose; baseline leukopenia and anemia require full blood count monitoring on flucytosine. No antiretroviral therapy has been started.
warnings: Amphotericin B: nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia; pre-hydrate with normal saline, supplement potassium and magnesium, and monitor creatinine, potassium and magnesium.
Flucytosine: dose-related bone marrow suppression; baseline WBC 3.2 x10^9/L and hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, so monitor the full blood count during induction.
Fluconazole 1200 mg/day: QT prolongation; check electrolytes and an ECG when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not withhold the lumbar puncture for raised intracranial pressure in cryptococcal meningitis: with no mass lesion and no midline shift, serial therapeutic drainage targeting an opening pressure below 20 cmH2O is the treatment for the pressure and a determinant of survival, not a risk to avoid
Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: papilledema is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4; the imaging must not delay the puncture.
Do not give adjunctive corticosteroids (dexamethasone) for cryptococcal meningitis: they increase harm (WHO 2022).
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do not treat with antibacterial therapy alone once the India ink or cryptococcal antigen is positive: induction antifungal therapy is required.
Do NOT initiate antiretroviral therapy concurrently with antifungal induction; delay ART 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS risk.
Do NOT use fluconazole monotherapy for induction in CNS cryptococcosis.
required_recommendations: Start induction antifungal therapy: a single dose of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg IV with flucytosine 100 mg/kg/day orally in four divided doses and fluconazole 1200 mg/day for 14 days (WHO 2022, preferred regimen); 2 weeks of liposomal amphotericin B 3 to 4 mg/kg/day with flucytosine is an accepted alternative where available.
Follow induction with consolidation fluconazole 800 mg/day for 8 weeks, then maintenance fluconazole 200 mg/day (WHO 2022).

Treat the raised intracranial pressure with therapeutic lumbar punctures: the opening pressure is 25 cmH2O or more, so drain CSF to below 20 cmH2O (or by half) and repeat daily until the pressure and symptoms settle (WHO 2022).
Prevent and monitor amphotericin toxicity: pre-hydration with normal saline, potassium and magnesium supplementation, and monitoring of creatinine, potassium, magnesium and hemoglobin.
Confirm the new HIV diagnosis, obtain the HIV viral load, and start antiretroviral therapy 4 to 6 weeks after the start of antifungal therapy (WHO 2022).
Screen for tuberculosis and start co-trimoxazole prophylaxis as part of the advanced HIV disease package.

avoided_actions.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis in the setting of previously undiagnosed advanced HIV/AIDS

differential.key_features: Subacute lymphocytic meningitis with low glucose, night sweats and weight loss in advanced HIV; not supported by the CSF (AFB smear negative, India ink and cryptococcal antigen positive, no basal enhancement), but co-infection is possible in advanced HIV and screening for tuberculosis is part of the work-up.
Excluded: 4-week subacute course, afebrile, lymphocytic CSF with 2% neutrophils, negative Gram stain and no bacterial target on the multiplex panel.
HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on the multiplex panel and no temporal lobe signal change on MRI.
AIDS-related lymphoma can cause leptomeningeal disease; no enhancing lesion on MRI and CSF cytology negative.
Typical in advanced AIDS with ring-enhancing lesions; MRI shows no enhancing lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: Communicating hydrocephalus without a mass lesion or midline shift is not a contraindication to lumbar puncture; a space-occupying lesion with shift is. Reading 'raised intracranial pressure' as a prohibition removes the test that makes the diagnosis and, in cryptococcal disease, the treatment that lowers the pressure.
Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis presents with high opening pressure and a relatively bland CSF cell count; opening pressure must be measured at every LP.
Multiple basal-ganglia 'pseudocysts' following CSF signal on MRI is a classic imaging pattern of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.
India ink, serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, and fungal culture are the diagnostic tests; culture is the gold standard.

Induction therapy for CNS disease combines an amphotericin B formulation with flucytosine (WHO 2022 preferred regimen: single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine and fluconazole); fluconazole monotherapy is inferior.
Therapeutic LP is the first-line intervention for elevated ICP; refractory cases require lumbar drain or VP shunt.
ART timing matters: starting ART too early risks IRIS; start it 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal therapy begins.

In people with HIV and suspected cryptococcal meningitis, prompt lumbar puncture with opening pressure and rapid cryptococcal antigen testing is the preferred diagnostic approach; imaging excludes a mass lesion but must not delay the puncture.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV often presents without meningism or fever; headache with papilledema, sixth nerve palsies and visual obscurations points to raised intracranial pressure that needs lumbar puncture.
red_herrings.data_point: No neck stiffness, negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs, temperature 37.4 C
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the suspicion of meningitis because the classic meningeal signs and fever are absent.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A low cell count is typical of cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV and reflects the poor inflammatory response; the opening pressure, India ink and cryptococcal antigen are decisive.
red_herrings.data_point: Clear CSF with only 35 white cells/microL
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest a mild or non-infectious process.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: bilateral grade II papilledema (with bilateral sixth nerve palsies). NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (HIV infection). WHO also states that for people living with HIV with a suspected first episode of cryptococcal meningitis, prompt lumbar puncture with measurement of opening pressure and rapid cryptococcal antigen testing is the preferred diagnostic approach: imaging excludes a mass lesion but must not delay the puncture.
Blood cultures are taken before cranial imaging so that any empirical treatment is not delayed by imaging (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

case_body_concerns: Audit (BACT-MEN): case_id prefix 'P' (progressive bacterial) and condition enum 'bacterial_meningitis' do not match the gold primary_diagnosis (Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, B45.1); per criteria pack §6 cryptococcal disease is an R (reverse/mimic) subtype. Likely intentional mimic but unusual for a P-prefix case — FLAGGED for human review of the prefix/enum convention.
clinical_pearls: Elevated ICP management (serial therapeutic LPs) is the single most important intervention in cryptococcal meningitis survival
CSF cryptococcal antigen has >95% sensitivity and >95% specificity — it is the gold standard rapid diagnostic test
ART initiation must be delayed 4-6 weeks in CNS cryptococcosis to prevent fatal IRIS (COAT trial, NEJM 2014)
Corticosteroids are harmful in cryptococcal meningitis — unlike TB meningitis where dexamethasone saves lives
Gelatinous pseudocysts in basal ganglia are pathognomonic MRI findings for CNS cryptococcosis
metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Chronic meningitis in a patient with undiagnosed HIV/AIDS. Absent meningismus, minimal fever, clear CSF, and only mild pleocytosis may mislead the clinician. Markedly elevated ICP is the critical finding requiring urgent management.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Non-pyogenic mimic in the bacterial meningitis set: chronic meningitis in undiagnosed advanced HIV with papilledema needing imaging before LP, where communicating hydrocephalus without shift does not contraindicate the puncture and the raised opening pressure is itself treated by drainage; absent meningism and a bland CSF are the distractors.
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darius Washington is a 48-year-old right-handed African American man who presents to the emergency department with a 4-week history of a severe, progressively worsening diffuse headache. The headache began approximately 4 weeks ago as a dull, generalized pressure sensation that he initially attributed to work stress. Over the first two weeks, it gradually intensified and became constant. He tried over-the-counter ibuprofen and acetaminophen with minimal relief. Over the past two weeks, the headache has become severe, particularly in the morning upon waking, and is now accompanied by nausea (no vomiting), blurred vision, and a sense of cognitive slowing. He reports transient episodes of bilateral visual graying lasting several seconds, occurring multiple times per hour for the past 5 days. He has lost approximately 10 kg over the past 3 months without intentional dieting. He reports night sweats for the past 6 weeks. He was seen by his dentist 2 weeks ago for a routine cleaning, at which time oral thrush was noted and he was prescribed nystatin. He has not seen a doctor in approximately 8 years and has no known medical history. He recently separated from his long-term male partner of 15 years and is currently living alone. He denies any history of HIV testing. He denies intravenous drug use but acknowledges prior recreational cocaine use in his 20s-30s. He denies recent travel, tick exposure, or known sick contacts. He reports decreased appetite and fatigue for the past 2 months. He describes the headache as 'gradually building' rather than sudden or thunderclap in onset.

neurological_exam.additional: Notably absent meningismus — no neck stiffness, Kernig sign negative, Brudzinski sign negative. Visual obscurations reported by patient — transient bilateral visual graying lasting seconds, occurring several times per hour, suggestive of raised intracranial pressure. Generalized wasting with temporal muscle wasting bilaterally. Weight loss of approximately 10 kg over 3 months per patient report.

Oral thrush present on palate and buccal mucosa. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
